title: Tamsin and the Postcards
premise: Casper Fairweather, a bridge inspector whose marriage to Tamsin has calcified into careful silence, is hired to assess a crumbling viaduct in a remote coastal village — the last home of Maren Oduya, the final fluent speaker of Kessari, a language with no written form. When Maren asks Casper and Tamsin to become her last students, recording her words before the viaduct's demolition erases the village entirely, the couple is forced into an intimacy of shared learning they've avoided for years. Through postcards Maren dictates in Kessari — messages to the dead, to the sea, to versions of themselves — Casper and Tamsin begin translating not just a dying language but their own unsaid inventory. When Maren dies mid-lesson and the viaduct falls on schedule, Casper must choose between the safe silence he's built and speaking aloud, at last, what survival has cost them both; the book ends with Tamsin answering him in imperfect Kessari, the language surviving as a marriage rather than a monument.
about_author: Lior Lockridge is the pen name of a former structural engineer who spent a decade inspecting bridges along the northern coast before turning to fiction. Their work explores how people maintain load-bearing silences, and what collapses when the inspection finally comes.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. On a routine inspection of the Harrow Viaduct, Casper measures hairline fractures and thinks about the twelve years of his marriage in equivalent engineering terms — stress, fatigue, tolerable deflection. He catalogs three things he hasn't said to Tamsin this week alone. The beat is quiet dread disguised as professional competence.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At home, Tamsin organizes the kitchen with the precision of someone avoiding a conversation. She finds an old postcard from her late brother, unsent replies she drafted years ago, and realizes she and Casper have stopped fighting because they've stopped expecting answers. The emotional beat: loneliness inside companionship.

chapters.title: Assignment: Kilnwater
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The firm assigns Casper to the Kilnwater Viaduct, a condemned structure in a remote fishing village slated for demolition. The file notes an 'occupancy complication' — a resident refusing relocation. Casper accepts the job gladly; distance feels like relief. Beat: escape mistaken for solution.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Wouldn't Leave
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, arriving in Kilnwater. The village is half-empty, houses boarded like closed eyes. At the viaduct's base stands a small stone cottage directly in the fall zone, and in its garden, an old woman counting aloud in a language Casper doesn't recognize. She watches him measure her home without fear. Beat: first collision.

chapters.title: Maren Oduya
chapters.summary: Maren's POV (first appearance). Inside the cottage, walls papered with decades of postcards in a script no postal service ever used. Maren reflects on outliving everyone who could answer her, on the demolition notice she keeps under a teacup. She has decided something about the inspector. Beat: dignity sharpened into intent.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Maren corners Casper at the site office: she'll sign the relocation papers if he agrees to one condition — learn Kessari, all of it, before the viaduct comes down. Four months. He refuses, then can't stop thinking about it. That night he calls Tamsin and, for the first time in years, describes something fully. Beat: the hook set.

chapters.title: Tamsin Comes North
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Suspicious of the sudden phone-voice husband, Tamsin drives north unannounced and finds Casper sitting in Maren's garden being taught the word for 'threshold.' Instead of anger, she feels a pull she resents. Maren looks at her and says, in English, 'You are the second student. I was waiting.' Beat: the trap closes gently.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. First real lesson: Kessari has no word for 'alone' — only words for 'unheard' and 'unanswered.' Casper and Tamsin stumble through pronunciation while Maren corrects them with ruthless tenderness. Walking back to the inn, they laugh for the first time in years, then go silent, frightened by it. Beat: fragile thaw.

chapters.title: The Postcards Explained
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. She shows them the wall: every card is addressed to someone dead or gone — her mother, her drowned husband, the schoolchildren evacuated during the Relocation Years. Kessari was banned in schools; the postcards were her smuggling route, language hidden in plain pictures. Beat: history arriving as intimate grief.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Maren tells the story of the Relocation Years: families split, children punished for speaking, neighbors informing on neighbors. Her fluency survived because she stayed silent for thirty years, mouthing words only. Casper recognizes the shape of it — his own strategic silences — and is ashamed of the comparison. Beat: guilt as mirror.

chapters.title: Grammar of Avoidance
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin proves a better student than Casper, which unsettles them both. In lesson, Maren teaches the Kessari tense for 'things postponed indefinitely' — a full grammatical category. Tamsin hears her own marriage described in someone else's grammar and has to leave the room. Beat: language as accusation.

chapters.title: The Engineer's Doubt
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Back at the viaduct, Casper's inspection reveals worse numbers than the file claimed — the demolition timeline may accelerate. He sits on the report for two days, telling himself it's procedure. It's not; he's protecting the lessons. Beat: complicity begins, small and deniable.

chapters.title: A Postcard to No One
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren dictates her first postcard with the students as witnesses — addressed to her husband, forty years dead, describing the two strangers learning her words. She makes Casper write it down phonetically and reads it back until it sounds right. Then she burns the draft. 'The saying is the keeping,' she tells them. Beat: ritual established.

chapters.title: Village of the Half-Speakers
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin befriends elderly villagers who remember fragments of Kessari — a prayer, a curse, a lullaby's first line — but nothing whole. One man weeps when she repeats his grandmother's lullaby correctly. She begins collecting fragments in a notebook, understanding she's building something larger than lessons. Beat: stakes widen beyond Maren.

chapters.title: The Firm Calls
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. His supervisor demands the Kilnwater report; the accelerated timeline is confirmed — demolition moved up six weeks. Casper signs off knowing it shortens Maren's time. He doesn't tell her that night. The lie sits between him and Tamsin at dinner like a third chair. Beat: moral rot sets in.

chapters.title: Unanswered
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin discovers the revised date on Casper's laptop and says nothing — mirroring his silence, testing whether he'll confess. They orbit each other for days, both fluent now in postponement. Maren, watching them, remarks that Kessari died once already from exactly this. Beat: the theme turned inward.

chapters.title: The Word for Goodbye Properly
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. There is a Kessari phrase — 'saying farewell so completely that the leaving cannot undo it' — that takes three days of lessons to even approach. Maren explains she never said it to anyone: not to the evacuated, not to her husband before the water took him. She wants to say it once, correctly, before she dies. Beat: the book's central desire named.

chapters.title: Confession at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper finally tells Maren about the accelerated date. She is not angry; she says the language has been given deadlines before and outlived them all. But privately she begins teaching faster, longer days, her cough worsening. Casper starts secretly recording lessons beyond the official archive. Beat: urgency doubled by mortality.

chapters.title: Tamsin's Postcard
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Maren asks Tamsin to dictate her own postcard — to her dead brother, the one she never answered. Writing it in broken Kessari, Tamsin finally grieves properly, aloud, in Maren's kitchen. Casper comes in mid-sentence and stays, listening, undone. Beat: the marriage's first true exchange in years, witnessed.

chapters.title: The Archive People
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. University linguists arrive to digitize Maren, treating her as data — hours of prompts, word lists, elicitations. Maren performs patiently, then dismisses them early and teaches the Fairweathers instead, unprompted, unpaid. 'They want the language,' she says. 'You need it. Those are different hungers.' Beat: the meaning of the project clarified.

chapters.title: Midpoint: The Falling Test
chapters.summary: Both POVs. A storm closes the coast road; power fails; the four sit by lamplight while the viaduct groans overhead. Maren tells the Kessari story of the bridge that sang before it fell — a warning song the elders could read. Casper realizes the structure's sounds match the story. The language was also engineering. Beat: wonder; the language is knowledge, not nostalgia.

chapters.title: Load-Bearing Silence
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper inspects the viaduct after the storm and finds damage that changes everything: it may fail before the controlled demolition, endangering the village side where Maren refuses to leave. He faces the choice he's been rehearsing all book — report truth and speed up everything, or manage it quietly. Beat: the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: He Tells Her Everything
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Casper confesses — the delayed report, the hidden recordings, the childhood stammer beaten into silence by a father who measured him too. Tamsin listens without rescuing him. For the first time they fight, loudly, in Kessari fragments and English, and it feels like weather breaking a drought. Beat: conflict as intimacy.

chapters.title: Evacuation Order
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Officialdom responds: mandatory evacuation of the fall zone, Maren's cottage included, effective in ten days. Maren signs nothing. The village splits — some beg her to go, others gather at her fence in quiet solidarity. Casper is asked by both sides to intervene. Beat: external pressure peaks.

chapters.title: The Last Full Lesson
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Knowing time is short, Maren abandons curriculum and teaches what matters: the phrases for birth, apology, forgiveness, and the long goodbye. She tells them the language will live only if it lives in use, not archives. She names Casper and Tamsin, formally, as speakers. Beat: transmission completed; weight transferred.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Evacuation day. Maren sits in her garden with tea. Tamsin stays beside her; Casper stands between them and the officials, buying hours with technical jargon about vibration monitoring. It works for a day. Tamsin realizes Casper has changed — the man who managed reports now spends truth like currency. Beat: love demonstrated through action.

chapters.title: The Compromise
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper negotiates: Maren gets seven days in the cottage under continuous structural watch, then goes. He knows he's gambling his career and possibly her life. Tamsin disagrees with the gamble but stands with him. Maren calls it, in Kessari, 'a bargain between people who have run out of cleverness.' Beat: stakes locked in.

chapters.title: Six Days of Saying
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs, compressed montage. Each day a theme: day one, names; day two, apologies; day three, the sea; day four, the dead; day five, love; day six, goodbye. Villagers come with fragments to be completed. Casper records; Tamsin transcribes; Maren pours herself out like light. Beat: elegiac acceleration.

chapters.title: The Cough
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Maren's cough turns wet; a doctor comes and goes grim-faced. Maren forbids hospitals: 'I will not spend my last words on forms.' Tamsin nurses her, learning the vocabulary of care in two languages. Casper paces the viaduct deck above, listening to it sing. Beat: two clocks converging — the body and the bridge.

chapters.title: What the Bridge Sang
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Night inspection: the wind finds a frequency and the viaduct hums the warning pattern from Maren's story. Casper verifies the numbers — failure window shorter than promised. Seven days becomes three. He must tell a dying woman her time is halved. Beat: dread crystallized.

chapters.title: Three Days
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Told the news, Maren laughs — genuinely — and revises her plan. 'Then we skip to the end of the alphabet.' She compresses the remaining teachings into essentials, prioritizing the long goodbye above all. She asks Casper and Tamsin to promise to speak to each other in Kessari after she's gone, badly, daily. Beat: the request that will bind the ending.

chapters.title: The Unsent Card
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Going through Maren's wall, Casper finds one blank postcard, stamped, addressed to no one — the one she couldn't finish. She asks him to write it for her, in whatever language he chooses, saying whatever he owes. He writes to his father. He does not burn this one. Beat: Casper's private climax approaches.

chapters.title: Day Before Demolition
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The village gathers for a last supper in the fall zone — illegal, joyous, candlelit beneath the dying bridge. Old men sing the recovered lullaby complete. Maren, frail, presides. Tamsin looks at Casper across the table and understands she is watching the end of something and the beginning of something else simultaneously. Beat: communal grace before loss.

chapters.title: The Long Goodbye, Spoken
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Dawn. In the garden, before the crews arrive, Maren speaks the full farewell phrase — to her dead, to the village, to the sea, and last to Casper and Tamsin, naming them speakers of Kessari. It takes eleven minutes. No one moves. When she finishes, she says in English: 'Now it cannot be undone.' Beat: the title's promise fulfilled.

chapters.title: Collapse
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The controlled demolition goes wrong at the margins — a section drops early toward the cottage side. Casper, ignoring every protocol, runs the evacuation himself, carrying Maren as the viaduct comes down behind them in a sound she describes, breathless, in Kessari: the singing, then the silence after. Beat: climax; action fused with meaning.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Dust settles over the village. Maren survives the collapse but not the week; she dies on the third morning with both students holding her hands, and her last word is not Kessari but Tamsin's name, said perfectly. The grief is enormous and clean — nothing unsaid. Beat: loss without regret, the book's thesis embodied.

chapters.title: The Inquiry
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The firm investigates Casper's report delays and unauthorized evacuation. He testifies plainly, owning every choice, and loses his license. Walking out of the hearing, he feels lighter than he has in twenty years. Some things survive demolition; some careers don't deserve to. Beat: the price paid, accepted.

chapters.title: The Wall Comes Down
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Packing the cottage, they take Maren's postcards to the archive — except the blank-finished one Casper wrote, which Tamsin quietly mails to his father's old address, where a sister still lives. The archive boxes close. Tamsin keeps one card back: Maren's last dictated message, untranslated. Beat: inheritance distributed.

chapters.title: Speaking Badly, Daily
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Home again, the Fairweathers keep the promise: Kessari at breakfast, mangled and mispronounced, greeting each other with the word for 'unheard' until neither is. Casper begins teaching a Saturday class of interested strangers from Tamsin's fragment notebook. The language lives in use, badly, daily — exactly as instructed. Beat: resolution through practice.

chapters.title: The Answer
chapters.summary: Both POVs, converging. A year later, at the sea near Kilnwater, Casper finally says the long goodbye phrase aloud — not to Maren but to Tamsin, ending the old marriage's silence formally so the new one can begin. Tamsin answers in imperfect Kessari, then translates herself into English so there can be no mistake. The tide comes in. Beat: full-circle closure; the language survives as love.
